headline: Gloucester's Cool Water Wins This Week: Bass on Bunker, Blues in the Wash
subhead: With Boston Harbor pushing into the mid-70s and stripers going nocturnal, the daylight bite belongs to Cape Ann and the North Shore rips.
body_markdown:
Every July I get to this same fork in the road, and this week it sent me north instead of into the Harbor. Deer Island and President Roads are still fishable, but the water inside has crept into the low-to-mid 70s, and that's the kind of number that pushes big bass off the daytime bite and onto the clock — feeding hard after dark, sulking on structure when the sun's up. North of the Cape, the Gulf of Maine keeps its hand on the thermostat. Nahant, Gloucester, Cape Ann — that water's running cooler, and the bass up there are still eating in daylight. So that's where I put my morning.

Egg Rock off Nahant was the first stop, first light, dead low into the first hour of the flood. Bass were sitting on the down-current side of the reef, ambushing whatever the tide pushed off the rocks. Ten-inch pencil poppers and 2-ounce Deadly Dicks worked the shallow edge, and we picked up school bass to 28 inches along with two that pushed past 34 — good fish for a rockpile bite, not blitz numbers, but steady enough to keep casting. The pattern held: cast tight to the rock, let it sink two counts, work it back with a walk-the-dog retrieve. Anything worked too fast in that current just skips over their heads.

Gloucester and the Dogbar Breakwater are where the week's real story is. Bunker schools — pogies, thick ones — have pushed up along the North Shore beaches and into the harbor mouth, and the bluefish have found them exactly like we said they would. We flagged this last week: bluefish would follow the bait up the coast, and here it is, playing out at Dogbar and along Good Harbor Beach with blues busting bait on the surface most mornings before 8. Wire leader is not optional right now — I lost two topwater plugs to bite-offs before I wised up. Kastmasters and 2-ounce Hopkins in chrome, cast into the froth, worked fast. These aren't cocktail blues either — some three and four pounders mixed in, chopping bait into pieces you can see from the rocks.

Thacher Island's rip, on the last two hours of the outgoing, gave up the better bass of the week — one at 41 inches on a live mackerel drifted back on a fish-finder rig, 20 feet of water, current ripping. That mackerel run has been the difference maker all month. If you can jig up a dozen off the boat — and they're still thick enough around Cape Ann to do that in twenty minutes — you've got the best bait in the water for anything from schoolies to the 40-inch class fish that are starting to show as the bunker draws bigger predators tight to structure.

apital move for me back down in the Harbor: I fished the Graves at last light instead of midday, live-lining a pogie on a slip float over the ledge in 35 feet as the tide started to drop. That's the nocturnal shift Hooper's data pointed to — warm surface water during the day, but a strong tide-driven thermocline kicking in as the sun goes down, and the bigger bass moving up onto structure to feed once it cools. Two fish over 36 inches in about ninety minutes of dark, both released. If you're committed to Boston Harbor stripers right now, that's the play — evening into dark, live bait over structure like Deer Island Light, The Graves, or the drop north of Calf Island, not midday jigging.

Flounder are still around for anyone who wants a change of pace and dinner. Winthrop flats and the mud inside Hingham Bay are giving up decent numbers on sandworms and skimmer clam, fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig with small spinners ahead of the hooks. Incoming tide, first two hours, is when they feed hardest over that soft bottom.

Down south toward Plymouth and Duxbury Bay, the pattern's mixed. The Gurnet rip has bass, but they're spread thin and the bite's been a night-tide thing more than anything reliable in daylight — similar warm-water story to the Harbor. Kingston Bay has bunker pushing in too, which should eventually pull blues down that way if the pattern holds, but as of this week it hasn't fully arrived. I'd give that another week before making a special trip.

Looking ahead, the moon's easing toward first quarter on the 21st, which means softer currents through the weekend — good news for anyone working live bait on structure, since a slower drift keeps the mackerel or pogie in the strike zone longer instead of getting ripped through on a hard tide. If the stable weather holds and that bunker stays put along the North Shore, I'd expect the bluefish blitzes at Dogbar and Good Harbor to keep going through the week. For bass, I'm sticking with my read: daylight structure fishing north of the Cape, nighttime live-bait drifts in the Harbor. That's where I'd spend my next trip, and I wouldn't change it unless that Gulf of Maine water starts warming faster than it has been.
